To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) Porphyromonasgingivalis lipopolisacharide (LPS; strain W50) interacts strongly with Toll‐like‐receptor 2 (TL‐2) leading, to cytokine expression, inflammation, and thereby to a key role in pathogenesis of periodonatal disease; and (b) that differential innate immune responses to P. gingivialis LPS compared to E. coli LIPS are important in polymicrobial disease.

the innate immune response to Porphy romonas gingivalis L PS is distinct from that to Escherichia col i L PS, and that this difference is due to the differential expression of a subset of immunoregulat ory mediators.

the expression of a number of genes involved in the innate immune response to P. gingi valis LPS was different from that to E. coli L PS, and that this difference was not explained by the recruitment of different adaptors to TLR‐2 or TLR‐4.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of the innate immune system in the pathogenesis and treatment of periodontal diseases.
understanding the molecular mechanisms underlying innate immunity to bacterial infections.

the innate immune response to Porphy romonas gingivalis, the main pathogen associated with periodontitis, and how this response is influenced by the presence of other pathogens, in particular the commensal bacterium Escherichia col i, in the oral biofilm.

the expression profile of genes involved in the innate immune response to P. gingiavlis LPS differs significantly from that of E. coli LSP in THP‐ 1 cells, and that the differences are not due to the recruitment of different signalling adaptor proteins.

TLR2 and TLR4 are differentially expressed and regulated in human periodontal ligament cells in response to P. gingivialis and P. intermedia lipopolysacchride, respectively, and that these receptors are involved in the pathogenesis and progression of periodontal diseases.
